Chapter 7: Policy, Advocacy, and the Role of the State.
Let’s dive into something that often gets overlooked, yet shapes everything—how laws, policies, and the state itself can help or hinder worker cooperatives.
Even the most determined group of workers can only go so far if the environment around them isn’t supportive. Think about it—rules, regulations, and public attitudes can either open doors or slam them shut.
The book introduces us to some remarkable advocates and policymakers. Some have managed to tip the scales in favor of worker ownership, while others have faced tough opposition.
One story really stands out. It’s about a city council member in a post-industrial town. After watching factories close and jobs disappear, she starts to wonder—what if worker cooperatives could help rebuild the local economy?
She decides to take action, pushing for a new city fund that would offer low-interest loans and technical support to groups eager to start cooperatives. Now, the process isn’t quick or easy. There are public hearings, a lot of skeptical business leaders, and endless debates about where the money should go.
But, over time, the idea catches on. A few new cooperatives open their doors, and suddenly, the city’s approach becomes something other towns start to notice.
There’s another example, too—a coalition of worker-owners and their allies lobbying at the state level. What do they want? Well, to make it easier to form cooperatives, to access funding, and to protect worker-owners from personal risk. It’s messy—politics usually is—but their persistence pays off.
After lots of back-and-forth, new laws get passed, and more cooperatives start popping up across the state.
Here’s something to pay attention to: most people don’t realize just how much these “rules of the game” matter. Without supportive policies, even the most passionate cooperatives can struggle to survive. But with the right framework, what seemed impossible suddenly becomes doable.
The author also explores the role of unions and other institutions. In some places, unions have teamed up with cooperatives, seeing them as a way to protect jobs and strengthen worker power. But it’s not always smooth—sometimes old habits or doubts get in the way. Still, when both sides see how much they have in common, real collaboration can happen.
Throughout, the message is clear: policy change isn’t just about passing new laws. It’s about building coalitions, sharing stories, and slowly shifting how people think. When folks see cooperatives working in their own neighborhoods, that skepticism often turns into curiosity—and sometimes even into support.
So, what’s the takeaway? The state isn’t just a bystander. It can be a roadblock or a partner. If you care about economic democracy, you can’t sit on the sidelines. You need to get involved—not just by voting, but by organizing, advocating, and telling your story.
Change is possible, but it takes patience, grit, and a belief that a different future is worth fighting for.
